rules.surface_condition: Left token is a numeral (contains a digit) and the token immediately after the cut is a unit/range connector (evidence of a number+unit or numeric range being split).
rules.blamed_rule: - Left or right stretch that ends or begins with a lexical token translators typically render reliably will tend to raise the measured value. Examples of such surface forms: numerals and formatted numbers (e.g., "1,200", "2050"), explicit dates, percentages, currency figures, and short fixed named phrases (e.g., organization names, place names). (Prediction to test: cuts adjacent to numerals/dates often score high.)
rules.proposed_rule: If the token immediately BEFORE the marker is NUM and the token immediately AFTER the marker is a unit or range connector (see check), move the score down into a lower band (e.g. target band 0–60) so the cut does not get ranked above intact number+unit/range boundaries.

rules.surface_condition: The token immediately AFTER the cut is a bare predicate-token (base verb or short adjective commonly starting the clause continuation), so the right side looks like a predicate that completes the left NP.
rules.blamed_rule: - Cuts that separate two independently meaningful lexical clusters (e.g., noun phrase + independent verb phrase) where both clusters contain content words (nouns, verbs, numerals) and do not leave a dangling single function word are likely to score higher. (Prediction to test: cuts after a main verb or after a multi-word noun phrase with a numeral/name often score high.)
rules.proposed_rule: If the token immediately AFTER the marker is one of short predicate starters (see check), lower the score (target band ~0–60) because the right side is likely a predicate that needs the left NP and standalone translation quality of the right fragment is often poor.

rules.surface_condition: The cut abuts parenthetical material / an opened parenthesis token (either the token immediately BEFORE or immediately AFTER the marker is the inner token of a parenthesis in the source).
rules.blamed_rule: - A marker that falls where a comma or parenthetical comma surrounds a self-contained adjunct (e.g., "yesterday,", "on Tuesday,", "as sources said,") often yields high scores if both sides can be translated faithfully by themselves. (Prediction to test: cuts after a comma that closes an embedded adjunct can score high.)
rules.proposed_rule: If the token immediately BEFORE or AFTER the marker is the inner token of parenthetical material (see check), reduce the score (target band 0–60). Parentheticals frequently tie tokens that belong together; cutting adjacent to them is often fragmentary or causes entailment errors.

tie_fix: The model produces equal scores when it applies identical surface heuristics to repeated/parallel tokens (e.g. multiple occurrences of the same function word). Break ties deterministically by preferring cuts that keep multi-token named expressions or number+unit pairs intact (i.e., when heuristics tie, rank cuts that do NOT split NUM+unit or NameName lower).
summary: The scorer systematically over-weights isolated lexical cues (numbers, names, parenthetical cues, bare predicate tokens) and thus ranks cuts that split number+unit pairs, parentheticals, or NP→predicate boundaries too highly. Applying targeted downward adjustments when a cut splits a numeral from its unit, when the right side begins with a bare predicate token, or when the cut abuts parenthetical inner tokens will reduce the label-vs-model ordering errors. The blamed lines in the prompt are the high-score suggestions for numerals, for separating lexical clusters, and for parentheticals — re-anchoring those tendencies to avoid splitting tightly-bound tokens fixes the observed errors.
